item.title: Effective transport statistics for cooperative molecular motor ensembles with tether slack
item.description: arXiv:2610.15152v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We improve upon our previous work using asymptotic analysis to characterize analytically the effective transport properties of a stochastic model for an ensemble of a cargo being pulled by two molecular motors walking on a microtubule. The governing equations are a system of stochastic differential equations with stochastic switching due to attachment and detachment kinetics of the molecular motors from the microtubule. Our model adopts a nonlinear tether which exerts no force when end-to-end distances are sufficiently small. This challenges some of the scale separation arguments from our previous work, and we modify the asymptotic analysis accordingly. In particular, spatial dynamics of the molecular motors may not always reach their quasi-stationary distribution within a particular attachment state. Rather, molecular motors tend to have a slack connection to the cargo for a while after they reattach, and we incorporate some first passage time analysis to determine if the tether becomes taut again. Through these and other modifications to the asymptotic analysis argument, the theoretical statistics for the run length, run time, and velocity of the motor-cargo ensemble can be brought into reasonable agreement with direct model simulations of two-motor ensembles consisting of kinesin-1 and kinesin-2. Additionally, we propose a new data fitting approach to obtain a double-exponential parameterization for the detachment rate of a motor as a function of the momentary force on its tether to the cargo, which is continuous at low load. Such a modified parameterization is needed to avoid artifacts in theoretical modeling of intracellular transport.
item.dc:creator: Joseph Klobusicky, John Fricks, Peter R. Kramer

item.title: Enforcing Thermodynamic Consistency in Parameter Optimization and Bayesian Inference of Biochemical Reaction Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.17155v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Subcellular signaling pathways regulating, e.g., cell division or synaptic plasticity, are often modeled as dynamical networks of reactions satisfying the law of mass action. To remain physically grounded, these models must satisfy different physical conservation laws, such as conservation of energy. This gives rise to thermodynamic constraints formalized by the Wegscheider conditions, which ensure that the system is in detailed balance at thermodynamic equilibrium. Explicitly imposing Wegscheider conditions requires identifying cycles in the reaction network. This can become computationally cumbersome, especially in large, complex systems. Furthermore, even when these constraints are explicitly available, enforcing them requires choosing a reparameterization of the network, which may introduce asymmetries among the parameters and affect numerical conditioning. Moreover, this approach often causes inverse uncertainty quantification methods like Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to struggle. Instead of imposing Wegscheider conditions directly in the parameter space, we propose an approach for promoting physical consistency by penalizing parameters that violate detailed balance. We first illustrate the approach on a simple reaction network containing a single cycle. We show that parameter values inferred without thermodynamic constraints can reproduce the experimental data seemingly accurately, while substantially violating the Wegscheider condition. In contrast, the proposed approach preserves the agreement with the observed dynamics while yielding posterior samples that approximately satisfy the thermodynamic constraint. We further apply the approach to a model of PKA-calcineurin signaling in synaptic long-term depression, demonstrating its applicability to a more complex biochemical reaction network.
item.dc:creator: Federica Milinanni, Andrei Kramer-Miehe, Jan Glaubitz, Olivia Eriksson

item.title: A Comprehensive Review on RNA Subcellular Localization Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2504.17162v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The subcellular localization of RNAs, including long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), messenger RNAs (mRNAs), microRNAs (miRNAs) and other smaller RNAs, plays a critical role in determining their biological functions. For instance, lncRNAs are predominantly associated with chromatin and act as regulators of gene transcription and chromatin structure, while mRNAs are distributed across the nucleus and cytoplasm, facilitating the transport of genetic information for protein synthesis. Understanding RNA localization sheds light on processes like gene expression regulation with spatial and temporal precision. However, traditional wet lab methods for determining RNA localization, such as in situ hybridization, are often time-consuming, resource-demanding, and costly. To overcome these challenges, computational methods leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) have emerged as powerful alternatives, enabling large-scale prediction of RNA subcellular localization. This paper provides a comprehensive review of the latest advancements in AI-based approaches for RNA subcellular localization prediction, covering various RNA types and focusing on sequence-based, image-based, and hybrid methodologies that combine both data types. We highlight the potential of these methods to accelerate RNA research, uncover molecular pathways, and guide targeted disease treatments. Furthermore, we critically discuss the challenges in AI/ML approaches for RNA subcellular localization, such as data scarcity and lack of benchmarks, and opportunities to address them. This review aims to serve as a valuable resource for researchers seeking to develop innovative solutions in the field of RNA subcellular localization and beyond.
item.dc:creator: Cece Zhang, Xuehuan Zhu, Nick Peterson, Jieqiong Wang, Shibiao Wan
